title: Assemble the Report
content:
What problem does this solve?
Lesson 2 created named data. Now you turn changing values into a readable field report. An f-string keeps the sentence shape fixed while the numbers and names inside it update.

Basic syntax
  f"Expedition {expedition}: {days_overdue} days overdue"

What actually happens
An f-string is a string with f before the opening quote. At runtime Python finds each {expression}, evaluates it, converts the result to text, and inserts it into the surrounding string. Braces can hold a single name or a small expression.

Last lesson you printed values on separate lines. An f-string builds one coherent message: f"Party registered: {registered}". That is clearer than gluing pieces with + or relying only on print's multiple arguments.

When this is useful
Use an f-string when the message has a fixed shape and the values inside it change.
concepts: A string is text in quotes
f-strings start with f before the opening quote
Expressions inside {} are evaluated and embedded
Prefer f-strings for formatted messages once you know the values' names

examples.title: Report
examples.explanation: Python substitutes the current values of expedition and days_overdue into one readable line.

examples.title: Forgot the leading f
examples.explanation: Without the f, braces print literally. The output is Status: {status}, not Status: OVERDUE.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the leading f — then {status} prints literally
Putting quotes incorrectly inside the braces
Hardcoding numbers into the message instead of inserting the variable names

exercises.title: Predict the report
hints: Substitute the braced expression with its value.
Keep the surrounding words and spaces exactly.
registered becomes 4 inside the finished string.

exercises.title: Repair the template
exercises.prompt:
This program is supposed to print:
Status: OVERDUE

It currently prints the braces literally. Fix it.
hints: An f-string starts with f immediately before the quote.
The braces should contain the variable name, not extra quotes.
Turn the printed string into an f-string so {status} is replaced.

tests.message: Use an f-string that includes status inside braces — do not hardcode OVERDUE in the print.

exercises.title: Build the dispatch line
exercises.prompt:
The variables are already created. Print exactly one line:
Expedition 17 | Party 4 | 3 days overdue

Build that line with an f-string so expedition, registered, and days_overdue come from the variables — do not hardcode those numbers in the printed string.
exercises.starter_code:
expedition = 17
registered = 4
days_overdue = 3
# Print the dispatch line
hints: Start your string with f and put expressions in braces.
Keep the pipes, spaces, and wording exactly as shown.
The f-string should mention expedition, registered, and days_overdue inside braces.

tests.message: Use an f-string that includes expedition, registered, and days_overdue in braces.

exercises.success_message: Dispatch line assembled. Variables, a string template, and print now work as one small program.
